title: DDIM-NLL: likelihood from the DDIM trajectory via instantaneous change-of-variables
one_liner: Attach a Hutchinson-trace change-of-variables term to the DDIM steps already taken during sampling, so negative log-likelihood comes at the marginal cost of one Jacobian-vector product per step.
description: DDIM sampling is deterministic: it is an Euler-style discretization of the probability flow ODE, so the log-density of a generated x_0 is the log-density of the initial noise plus the accumulated log-|det| of the drift's Jacobian along that same trajectory. The DDIM paper left NLL unevaluated only because it treated likelihood as needing a separate inference pass; the instantaneous change-of-variables formula supplies it for free inside the existing sampling loop. At each step we already compute the drift v_θ(x_t, t); we add Δt·div(v), with the divergence estimated by Hutchinson's random-projection trace estimator (one backward-mode vjp through the score network per step). This gives an approximate NLL that is exact in the continuous limit, at essentially the cost of the sampling run itself, and — unlike a separately-solved fine ODE — it reports likelihood for the very sampler the model deploys.

sections.technique: Take a trained DDIM ε-prediction model and a fixed T-step schedule. In the sampling loop, at each step: (1) compute the standard DDIM drift v_θ(x_t,t); (2) draw z ~ N(0,I), compute zᵀ J_v z via one vjp through the score network, average over k=1–4 projections for variance control; (3) accumulate the divergence term into a running log-Jacobian sum; (4) at the end add log-density of x_T under N(0,I). Report NLL = -(sum + log p(x_T)). Validate by comparing against (a) the Score-SDE-style adaptive fine ODE solve as ground-truth continuous likelihood, (b) an importance-weighted lower bound on the reverse chain, and (c) NLL as a function of T (e.g., 10, 50, 100, 1000 steps) to quantify discretization bias.
open_questions: Does the discretization bias of DDIM's Euler steps corrupt the change-of-variables estimate, and does it converge to the continuous ODE likelihood as T grows or to some other quantity?
How many Hutchinson projections per step are needed to keep variance acceptable, and does the per-step vjp make this cheaper or more expensive than a fine-grained ODE solve at equal accuracy?
Which parameterization (ε-prediction vs. v-prediction vs. score) gives the drift that actually satisfies the change-of-variables identity, and does the answer change the estimate?
Should the divergence be accumulated along the pure deterministic DDIM path or along a predictor–corrector variant, and which one matches the model's reported sampling distribution?
Is the resulting NLL comparable to DDPM/Score-SDE NLL numbers given that DDIM's marginal is defined by the discretized map rather than the continuous SDE?
sections.rationale: Stance: combiner. I fuse DDIM (deterministic, few-step sampler with no likelihood access) with the instantaneous change-of-variables estimator from the probability-flow-ODE literature (exact likelihood, but normally requiring an expensive, separate, fine-grained ODE solve). The composition is the contribution: the estimator runs inside the DDIM loop and reuses its trajectory, so marginal cost is one extra JVP per step instead of a second inference pass. The naive stack — sample with DDIM, then run a separate fine ODE solver — is exactly the "simple way" the DDIM authors found missing: it doubles cost and estimates the likelihood of a different trajectory than the sampler actually produces; this pairing makes the estimate consistent with the deployed sampler, which is the efficiency win. Unverified claims from outside the provided context: (1) that DDIM's discrete steps correspond to discretizing the probability flow ODE in the sense required for change-of-variables; (2) that the Hutchinson/Skilling trace estimator plus instantaneous change-of-variables is the standard exact-likelihood method in the score-SDE literature; (3) that later ODE-sampler papers (e.g., EDM-style) compute NLL along their own deterministic trajectories rather than along DDIM specifically — if (3) is true, the novelty is narrow and the value is the cheap, sampler-consistent estimator rather than the general technique.
